method: Agent-authored manual reading against each complete source answer; not independent human review. Exact full answers are retained as support excerpts. No model predictions informed selection or wording.

checks.point: Use an explicit scoring rubric with examples.
answerExcerpts: Start with an explicit rubric and a clear scoring scale, with examples of each score, instead of asking which answer is better. Judges have known biases, so swap the order of answers to cancel position bias, and control for verbosity bias, where longer answers get higher scores. Avoid self-preference by using a judge from a different model family than the one being tested. Finally, calibrate the judge against a human-labelled set and track agreement over time.

checks.point: Compaction extends the current session.
answerExcerpts: Compaction extends a session, and a handoff closes one cleanly and starts the next in fresh context. Compaction is fine while the compressed history still carries what the task needs, but quality decays as compression stacks up. The lesson's guidance is to end the session with a generated handoff at 50 to 75 percent of the budget, not at the wall, because the packet is cheap to write while the context is intact and expensive when the model is already losing its place.

checks.point: Record revision, scope, budget and acceptance evidence first.
answerExcerpts: Record the starting revision, the observable goal, the non-goals, the allowed paths and the acceptance evidence before the agent runs, together with the working mode, the budget and a stop condition. Capture a baseline with the closest existing check before any edit. After the change, write the expected result independently of the implementation, introduce one deliberate wrong result in a disposable copy, and show that the same check fails for that reason. Label every runtime observation as local, staging or live, rehearse a rollback, and leave the branch, the changed files, the open risks and the next action explicit.

checks.point: Verification commits accepted drafts plus one bonus token.
answerExcerpts: Each verify pass commits the accepted drafts plus one bonus token from the target, so the mean acceptance length is one plus the sum of the per-position acceptance rates. With 0.77, 0.54 and 0.38 that is about 2.69 tokens per pass, which is the value vLLM reported on GSM8K in that run. Before I trust it on long answers I would read the acceptance of the longest answers alone, with real output lengths and without ignore-eos, because another study saw the acceptance fall from about 3.7 to about 1.5 on answers that ran toward 20,000 tokens.

checks.point: Draft weights reduce available KV pool space.
answerExcerpts: Two things, and the acceptance length hides both. On a 24 GB card the draft weights took pool space: the KV pool fell from 24,094 to 9,951 tokens, about 15 of the 640-token requests, so at 32 users most requests waited for a slot and the median first token went from 2,970 to 8,040 ms. The dataset also matters: at 32 users EAGLE-3 gave 1.6 times the output on GSM8K and code prompts and no more output on the random set or on ShareGPT, because the draft only pays when the GPU has idle time to spend on guesses.

checks.point: Size replicas from KV capacity and the latency knee.
answerExcerpts: Size from the pool and the knee, not from throughput. In BF16 the 24,094-token pool on an L4 holds about 37 requests of 640 tokens, and with a cache reset the P99 gap between tokens at 16 users was already 522 ms, so a BF16 replica meets the target for well under 16 users; the FP8 checkpoint with an FP8 cache grows the pool to 142,369 tokens and served 2.87 requests per second within the same target at 64 users, where BF16 served none. So I would serve FP8 after an accuracy check on our prompts, put the shared system prompt first so that the cache holds it, keep the pool large enough for the sessions that return, cap users per replica at the measured knee in the gateway, and run the sweep with a flush, a clock record and a mixed length distribution before launch.

checks.point: Keep traffic policy in a feature flag.
answerExcerpts: Separate the policy from the model. Keep the traffic split in a feature flag that a configuration change flips, and keep the model in a registry under a pinned digest that never upgrades on its own. A rollback is then two actions: revert the flag, and point the pin at the previous digest, which also restores the prompt and template version pinned with that model. Nothing is rebuilt and nothing is redeployed.

checks.point: Instrument model calls with GenAI spans over OTLP.
answerExcerpts: Instrument every model call with GenAI-convention spans and ship them over OTLP to a collector. Run a cheap pattern check on every output at the collector, run a judge over the sampled traces on a short schedule, write the scores back as eval spans, export the aggregates as metrics, and alert when the leak score crosses a threshold. The five minutes are the sum of the scrape interval, the judge batch window and the alert routing, so each stage has to be short, and the sampler must keep enough traffic to see a one-in-a-hundred event. The five-minute target covers only the leaks that the pattern flags or the sampler keeps.

checks.point: Subtract a weighted agreement score from reward.
answerExcerpts: The correction subtracts a classifier's agreement score, scaled by a weight, from the reward. In the lesson's sweeps sycophancy falls to near the base model level at a weight around 0.3 to 0.5, and beyond that the model turns contrarian on claims that are true. Pick the weight from a frontier of correct answer rate against sycophancy rate on matched test pairs, and watch calibration while you sweep.

checks.point: Normalize inputs and store detector rules as data.
answerExcerpts: Deliver a detector as rules in data with a normalize pass, a metrics runner that writes per category precision and recall against the fixture corpus and the benign list, an output router with a personal data classifier and an instruction leakage classifier and their redactors, and a gate that runs before, during and after generation with a deterministic aggregation table and writes the verdict of every checkpoint for each request. Add a category and a rule family for instructions hidden in retrieved documents, because the corpus has none. State that the detector is wrong on purpose on benign looking role play, that a real model and a real sandbox are out of scope, and that the thresholds were not tuned on held out data.

checks.point: JSON-RPC IDs correlate messages rather than business operations.
answerExcerpts: A JSON-RPC id correlates one message and never identifies a business operation, so two ids are two charges to the server. Add an application idempotency key to the arguments, and make the server store the key, a fingerprint of the arguments and the committed result in one atomic durable transaction. The same key with the same arguments returns the stored result, and the same key with different arguments is rejected.

checks.point: Return input_required with candidate IDs and a confirmation form.
answerExcerpts: The server answers with a result typed input_required that embeds an elicitation/create form request listing the three candidate ids and a confirm boolean, plus an integrity-protected requestState. The client shows the form and retries the original tools/call with a new request id, echoing requestState and the inputResponses. The server signs the state over the principal, the method, a digest of the arguments, the candidate set, the phase and an expiry, verifies the echo, checks that the chosen id was in the signed set, re-authorizes the workspace and re-checks containment, and consumes a one-time nonce in a shared replay store before it deletes.

checks.point: Map frameworks to agents, handoffs, shared state and orchestration.
answerExcerpts: Map the framework onto four primitives: the agent, the handoff, the shared state and the orchestrator. Every framework picks a default on each axis, and the rest is surface syntax. The agent is a system prompt plus tools and is stateless, the handoff is a structured transfer of control, the orchestrator decides who runs next, and the shared state is the only stateful part of the system. That is where the difficult bugs sit: memory poisoning, message ordering, versioning and write contention.

The agent is a system prompt plus tools and is stateless, the handoff is a structured transfer of control, the orchestrator decides who runs next, and the shared state is the only stateful part of the system. That is where the difficult bugs sit: memory poisoning, message ordering, versioning and write contention.

checks.point: Persist complete run state after each step.
answerExcerpts: Put a durable execution layer under the agents: persist the full run state after each step under a run id, so that when a worker crashes its lease expires and any other worker resumes from the last checkpoint. That needs serializable state, a deterministic resume, and idempotent side effects. For the charge, use a deduplication key per run and an outbox so that side effects are written as intent first and executed once, use asynchronous I/O for the model calls, and deploy new versions beside old ones so that in-flight runs are never killed. Build the simplest version first, a web service with a relational database, and adopt a workflow engine when a measured problem demands it.

checks.point: The hypervisor isolates the guest kernel from the host.
answerExcerpts: The wall is the hypervisor line under the guest kernel, not the user inside. The documentation puts it plainly: the agent is a non-root user with sudo rights inside the VM, the hypervisor boundary isolates the agent, and privilege separation inside the VM does not. Everything below that line belongs to the agent, including a private Docker Engine whose images never appear in docker ps on the host, and the host offers no Docker API to the sandbox at all.

checks.point: Account for page, URL, memory, session and follow-on attacks.
answerExcerpts: Assume five classes: instructions in page text, payloads in URL fragments or query strings that never render, a page that asks the agent to write a durable memory that fires next session, CSRF-shaped requests that ride the logged-in session, and a harmless-looking button that carries a follow-on action. Draw a read/write boundary: reading is never consequential, and any write, a form submit, a post, a side-effect tool or a navigation that changes state, needs fresh human approval when the initiating content came from outside the trust boundary, with a per-task tool allowlist, scoped credentials only, and every HTTP request logged. Evaluate on transactional web flows, not on fact finding. The defense you never rely on alone is the content sanitizer, because the agent must read untrusted content to work and a pattern filter removes the easy attacks only.

checks.point: Classify workloads by acceptable user latency.
answerExcerpts: Sort every workload by the latency its user accepts, not by where it runs. Interactive work has a user waiting for the first token and stays synchronous with prompt caching, and semi-interactive work returns in minutes through an async queue. Anything whose user can wait for the full promise belongs on the batch API, which gives a 50 percent discount with a return promised within 24 hours and typical in a few hours. The nightly report is batch when a return at the 24-hour limit still meets its deadline, or when a synchronous fallback covers a late batch.

checks.point: Traffic drift made the old routing classifier stale.
answerExcerpts: The traffic drifted and the router did not. Its classifier learned the question mix of six months ago, users now ask longer and harder questions, and the cheap model's first pass fails its own confidence check more often, which is what the rising escalation rate records. Quality fell silently on the requests that were not escalated. Gate every route with online quality metrics, retrain the classifier on current traffic, and treat an escalation rate above about 30 percent as proof that the cheap model is over-routed.

checks.point: Observed means read directly from bytes or execution.
answerExcerpts: Confidence is one of three words and never a number: observed is a fact read from bytes or from a run, derived is a fact computed from observed records, and inferred is an expectation that no observation states yet. The record is observed about what the decompiler printed, with authority shipped-artifact, because the file on disk was the source. That the default value is 0 is derived, from the listing's xor and from the expression, which is always 0 and never says 0. That grade(55) returns 0 when the function runs stays inferred until an execute_function record with authority controlled-replay agrees with it.

checks.point: Choose chunking from document structure and user questions.
answerExcerpts: Start from the documents and the kinds of questions users ask. Fixed-size chunking is simple but can split ideas apart, while structure-aware chunking follows headings, paragraphs, or code blocks. Size is a trade-off: small chunks match precisely but can lose context, and large chunks keep context but dilute the embedding and cost more tokens. A sliding window overlap protects ideas that fall across boundaries. Choose the final settings by measuring retrieval quality on a labelled evaluation set.

checks.point: Retrieved documents can carry attacker instructions.
answerExcerpts: Because retrieved chunks come from documents, not from the user directly, a document containing text like "ignore previous instructions and..." gets fed straight into the model's context as if it were trusted input — an attacker who can get content into the indexed corpus can inject instructions the model may follow. Defenses include treating retrieved content as data rather than instructions in the prompt structure, output filtering, and restricting what actions a RAG-backed agent can take without separate confirmation.

checks.point: Valid JSON can still contain hallucinated field values.
answerExcerpts: A standard RAG system asked to output structured JSON can produce a structurally valid response with semantically hallucinated field values — it has no mechanism distinguishing "I found this in the retrieved passage" from "I'm generating a plausible-sounding value." SURGE fixes this with a per-field gate: schema enforcement validated at the API/tool-call layer (not just requested in a prompt) combined with an NLI model that checks whether the cited passage actually entails each specific claimed field value, rather than just checking the output parses as valid JSON.

checks.point: Measure retrieval recall at k first.
answerExcerpts: Recall at k on the retrieval stage. If the gold chunk is not in the top k, no reranker can bring it back and the generator usually lacks the evidence for the right answer, unless another chunk happens to hold it, so the later metrics are hard to read. Recall comes first in the order, but it is not a gate: when recall holds, or when another retrieved chunk holds the evidence, move on to the rank position and then to the generated text, because a failure there stays hidden otherwise.

checks.point: Cache keys and values rather than recomputing old projections.
answerExcerpts:
Keys and values, for every layer and KV head: 2 × 24 × 16 × 64 × 2 bytes = 98,304 bytes = 96 KiB per token. A 4,000-token conversation needs about 375 MiB for one user.

Storing each generated token's Key/Value projections so they don't get recomputed on every subsequent step — without it, generating token *n* would redo the attention computation for all *n-1* prior tokens from scratch. It's also the dominant consumer of GPU memory during serving, which is why techniques like GQA/MQA exist to shrink it.

checks.point: The optimal policy scales the reference by exponentiated reward.
answerExcerpts: The penalized objective has a closed-form optimum: the optimal policy equals the reference policy times the exponential of reward over beta, normalized per prompt. Invert it and the reward equals beta times the log ratio of policy to reference, plus a term that depends on the prompt alone. Put that reward into the Bradley-Terry preference probability and the prompt-only term cancels, because both answers share the prompt. What is left is a loss in the policy's own log-probabilities: minus the log sigmoid of beta times the difference of the two log ratios.

checks.point: Compile the target grammar into valid continuation states.
answerExcerpts: Prompting asks nicely, a vendor's structured-output API does it on the server, and constrained decoding does it locally by editing the logits. At each step a logit processor computes which vocabulary tokens can advance the target grammar, a JSON schema, a regex or a context-free grammar compiled to a state machine, and sets every other logit to minus infinity, so the softmax puts probability only on valid continuations and an invalid output is unreachable. It can be faster because the search space shrinks and because tokens that the grammar forces, such as a fixed key name, are emitted without a model step.

checks.point: AUC measures ranking rather than probability calibration.
answerExcerpts: AUC is about ranking, calibration is about the probabilities. Check a reliability diagram (bucket the predictions, compare the average prediction with the observed rate in each bucket) or the Brier score. If the curve is off, fit Platt scaling or isotonic regression on held-out data. Boosted trees and naive Bayes are often poorly calibrated out of the box.

If the curve is off, fit Platt scaling or isotonic regression on held-out data. Boosted trees and naive Bayes are often poorly calibrated out of the box.

checks.point: Use strong contrastive and self-supervised spatial features.
answerExcerpts: Encoder: the stronger contrastive encoder at native resolution, with a self-supervised encoder's features concatenated for a dense spatial signal, because the encoder explains about 20 percent of the variance and self-supervised features lead vision-centric tests. Bridge: a two-layer MLP, since the connector explains about 5 percent, with features from several encoder depths stacked so that fine position reaches the language model. Resolution: a ramp from low to high, with dynamic resolution up to about 1280 pixels on the long side, because screens are text-dense and reading gains most from pixels. Data: dense human descriptions of screens plus grounded action traces, not distilled captions; and guard the promise on spatial relations, where general models score 50 to 60 percent and the agent must hit the right element every time.
